analysis.one_liner: Removes marijuana from the federal list of controlled substances, expunges past convictions, and reinvests tax revenue in affected communities.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill to decriminalize marijuana sat in the Finance Committee for a year and a half and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take marijuana off the federal controlled substances list, ending federal criminal penalties for making, selling, or possessing it. It would automatically wipe out federal marijuana convictions dating back to 1971, allow people still serving sentences to ask for shorter ones, and stop the government from denying federal benefits, security clearances, or immigration status over cannabis. It would also legalize a commercial cannabis market, funded by a new 5% federal sales tax whose revenue pays for job training, legal aid, and treatment in communities hit hardest by drug enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: People with federal marijuana convictions, who would get their records cleared automatically and could petition for shorter sentences. Anyone arrested or convicted for cannabis, who could no longer be denied federal benefits, security clearances, or immigration status because of it. Small cannabis businesses and their workers, who would gain access to Small Business Administration loans and services. And nonprofits in communities affected by the drug war, funded through a new trust fund for job training, reentry services, legal aid, literacy, youth programs, and substance use treatment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with cannabis records and affected communities

how_it_helps.text: Removes marijuana and THC from the controlled substances schedules and eliminates federal criminal penalties for manufacturing, distributing, or possessing marijuana, with the change applying retroactively.

Requires every federal court district, within one year, to expunge federal cannabis convictions from 1971 onward, including associated arrests, and lets people still under sentence seek a sentencing review with appointed counsel if indigent.

Creates an Opportunity Trust Fund funded by a 5% tax on cannabis products, with 60% going to grants for job training, reentry services, legal aid for expungement, literacy, youth programs, and substance use treatment for people most harmed by the drug war.
Bars federal agencies from denying public benefits, security clearances, or immigration benefits to anyone because of cannabis use, possession, or a cannabis conviction.
Makes Small Business Administration loans, microloans, disaster loans, and business counseling available to state-legal cannabis businesses that are currently excluded from them.

analysis.who_pays: Cannabis consumers and businesses would pay a new 5% federal excise tax, and cannabis manufacturers would face the same federal tax compliance regime as tobacco makers, including bonding requirements. Federal prosecutors and drug enforcement agencies would lose marijuana cases. States would remain responsible for setting their own rules for a newly legal market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cannabis consumers and small cannabis businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a new 5% federal excise tax on all cannabis products, which would raise prices for consumers and add tax-bonding and filing compliance costs for small growers and sellers, treating them like tobacco manufacturers.

Descheduling removes federal penalties without creating a single federal regulator for potency, labeling, or sales, leaving a patchwork of 50 state systems and pushing questions like driving rules and youth access to state legislatures.

The good-faith objection: opponents of legalization argue removing federal criminal penalties increases availability of a drug that remains illegal for people under 21, and that expunging millions of records creates a heavy, error-prone workload for federal courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial and targeted at people: erasing criminal records that block jobs, housing, benefits, and immigration status, and redirecting tax revenue into the communities where enforcement was concentrated. The costs are real but modest: a 5% consumer tax, compliance burdens on small cannabis businesses, and a one-time push for courts to process expungements. The tax was set low enough to keep the legal market competitive with the illegal one, which is the design choice that matters most.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee on July 23, 2019, and no committee or floor action ever followed, so it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Kamala Harris introduced the MORE Act in the Senate on July 23, 2019, joined by Senators Booker, Merkley, Wyden, and Warren.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced, and the record shows no further action — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote.
Eight senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill, but it never left committee before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal marijuana prohibition and its enforcement continued unchanged, no cannabis records were expunged, and no 5% cannabis tax was created. State-legal cannabis businesses continued to be shut out of Small Business Administration loans, and no money flowed to communities affected by the drug war.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal prohibition and its enforcement continued

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought a marijuana legalization bill to the Senate floor during the 116th Congress, leaving committee-referred bills to die.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter in the record — the sponsor and all eight cosponsors — was a Democrat, no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled Senate took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would give these businesses full legal status federally and open Small Business Administration loans and business-development services to them for the first time, ending their exclusion from banking-adjacent federal support. Ordinary consumers and people with records benefit alongside them from legalization, though the 5% tax channels public revenue through the new commercial market.

industries.industry: Reentry, legal aid, and substance-use-treatment nonprofits
industries.note: A new Community Reinvestment Grant Program, funded by the cannabis tax, would direct federal money to nonprofits providing job training, reentry services, legal aid for expungement, and treatment to people most harmed by the drug war.

Removing marijuana from the controlled substances schedules eliminates federal criminal penalties and the prosecutorial and enforcement role built around them, including wiretap and national-forest marijuana provisions. Its loss is the public's gain in this bill.
